titre: The World's Most Numerous Bird Vanished in Forty Years
accroche: Colonies of tens of millions, then none at all. Hunting does not explain everything: reproduction itself depended on those numbers.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1813, the ornithologist John James Audubon crosses Kentucky beneath a flight of passenger pigeons that darkens the sky all day long. He counts 163 flocks in 21 minutes and puts forward an estimate close to a billion birds for that single passage. Other naturalists of the time hold the species to be 25 to 40% of all land birds in the United States.

A century later, not one is left. Martha, the last of the species, dies at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914, at 1:00 p.m.

## The Mechanism

Commercial hunting explains a good part of the disaster: the meat sells cheap, nets and guns bring down thousands of birds a day, and the survivors stay bunched together even as their neighbors fall, which makes the slaughter easier still. Deforestation, for its part, deprives the species of the great oak and beech forests it drew its food from.

But hunting and deforestation do not explain why the final collapse, between 1870 and 1890, was so abrupt when millions of birds still existed. The passenger pigeon had adapted to living in immense colonies, sometimes numbering several tens of millions of individuals on a handful of square kilometers. Living in such great numbers was not a detail: reproduction itself depended on it, through a mechanism ecology now calls the Allee effect, in which a species' reproduction rate falls, rather than rises, below a certain density threshold. An isolated pair had trouble triggering egg laying; massed in the millions, by contrast, the whole colony nested at the same time, which limited losses to predators. When hunting shrank the colonies below that threshold, each season produced fewer young than the last, with no further pressure needed to finish off the decline.

## What Shifts

A century of abundance suggested the species was indestructible; it is precisely that abundance, organized into gigantic colonies, that made it brittle. A genetic study published in 2014 adds a nuance: even before European settlers arrived, the passenger pigeon population was already fluctuating widely with the years of acorns and beechnuts, at times dropping to a fraction of its peaks. It is possible that 19th-century hunting struck the species during one of these natural lows rather than at a high, which would make the collapse less surprising, and the lesson more worrying: a large population, measured on a given day, says nothing about its capacity to withstand sustained pressure.

carte.punch: Millions of passenger pigeons remained. Their reproduction had already collapsed.
carte.idee: The passenger pigeon bred in colonies of several tens of millions of individuals. Below a certain threshold, each brood produced fewer young than the last: the species went extinct with no further hunting needed. Martha, the last one, died in 1914.

quiz.question: Why does hunting alone not explain the abruptness of the very last phase of the passenger pigeon's decline?
choix: Because commercial hunting had stopped everywhere by 1870
Because below a certain density threshold, the colony could no longer reproduce
Because deforestation had stopped by that date
Because the species was already migrating entirely out of North America
quiz.explication: Hunting and deforestation continued after 1870. What precipitated the final collapse was the Allee effect: below a certain density threshold, the colony could no longer synchronize its egg laying, and each season produced fewer young than the last.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Audubon count in Kentucky in 1813 to estimate the scale of the passenger pigeon flight?
choix: The number of nests on a single branch
The total weight of birds caught in a day of hunting
The number of colonies recorded across the whole country
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Audubon counted 163 flocks of passenger pigeons in 21 minutes, which led him to put forward an estimate close to a billion birds for that single passage.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the genetic study published in 2014 add to the story of the passenger pigeon's extinction?
choix: It shows the species was never as numerous as believed
It shows that hunting had no real effect on the population
It shows that the population was already fluctuating widely before European settlers arrived
It shows that the Allee effect does not apply to this species
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2014 genetic study shows that even before European settlers arrived, the passenger pigeon population was already fluctuating widely with the years of acorns and beechnuts, sometimes dropping to a fraction of its peaks.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the Allee effect, as described in the card?
choix: A mechanism by which a species reproduces faster when it is threatened
A disease that specifically affects overly dense bird colonies
A migratory phenomenon triggered by dwindling food
A mechanism by which a species' reproduction rate falls below a certain density threshold
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Allee effect describes a species whose reproduction rate falls, rather than rises, below a certain density threshold: an isolated pair has trouble triggering egg laying, unlike a massed colony.
